rows.text: Polish that cup until you can see your face in it, then go and find an empty shelf.
I will not sulk in the trophy room, {winner}, because the carpet deserves better.
Neither of us lifts it, so the room gets a fresh cloth and a shrug.
Honestly, the trophies do most of the talking. I just keep the ribbons straight.
Keep the key safe for me, {winner}, and do not let it get used as a bottle opener.
Nobody gets the glory from a draw, so the least we can do is split the dusting.
Engraving takes ages, so I told the engraver to leave room for my middle name.
Next season I will bring my own cloth, and the silver will know exactly who is coming.
A draw keeps the cabinet locked, and I have not decided whether to thank or blame the key.
Forget the medals, I am in it for the squeak the cabinet door makes when it opens.
Your display is gleaming, {winner}, and I am jealous in the most respectful way.
The lock sticks, so every time I open the doors I make a proper performance of it.
Nobody takes the big gold cup today, so we get to glare at it together, politely.
Engraved silver is lovely, but the best part is seeing my name spelled right for once.
I have dusted the ribbons again and again, which tells you exactly how I took the news.
A draw hands us the same view of the silver, and gloating is off the menu.
Trophies are only metal until somebody polishes them, so I keep a cloth in my pocket.
Well played, {winner}. Please tell the cabinet it can stop looking so smug about it.
A draw means the key stays in my pocket and yours, which is a very polite standoff.
The trophy room smells of polish and fresh victory, and I am glad to be its tenant.
Those medals look far too good on someone else, so I shall plan my revenge with a feather duster.
Every proud manager needs a locked door, a warm light and a rival who asks to see inside.
We both polish until the silver shows our faces, and nobody can say who looks better.
I have a shelf for every season, a drawer for the medals and a ribbon for the bad days.
Your name on that plate looks very grand, {winner}, so I will read it while I make tea.
A draw will not hand either of us a trophy, but it does hand us a duster and a grin.
Anyone can own a key, {loser}, but only a true champion remembers where the spare is.
My shelf has room for improvement, so I am spending the next few evenings with a saw.
No trophy moves tonight, so the room can finally have a sit down and so can we.
Gold in the case, silver in the drawer, and a grin so wide it needs its own shelf.
The engraving on that plate is so neat, {winner}, that I am tempted to resent it quietly.
Keep the cabinet door shut on the cup, or the whole house will start bragging for me.
Honest managers polish their own silver, and a draw keeps us both honest.
Every medal has its own ribbon, every ribbon has its own admirer, and the admirer is me.
{winner} has the nicer display, but I have the nicer excuses, so we are even.
The silver goes back in its velvet box and our bragging rights go back in our pockets.
Medals only shine when someone bothers, and I have always been the bothering type.
The spare key hangs round my neck on a ribbon, and I am not giving it back to you, {winner}.
Nobody claims the top shelf today, so we will both pretend that was our plan all along.
Put the cup on the top shelf and let the lamp do the bragging while I sit back.
Your trophy room dazzles, {winner}, and I have already sketched the shelves I want.
Silver tarnishes if you ignore it, which is why I check on mine every morning without fail.
We cannot both lift the silver, so the glass gets polished and the bragging stays even.
The case and I have an understanding, and the little plaque on the door is the proof.
Losing gracefully is hard to practise, but I am getting better at it, dusting shelves each night.
Grins are free in a draw, and the trophy room is getting a double helping of both.
The whole room hums when the lamp is on, like an old jukebox that only plays my songs.
Another season is on the books, and my wallet has started asking for a bigger cabinet.
Neither the key nor the trophy changes hands, so we both just nod at the shelves.
Most of the fun is the dusting, and the rest is bragging, which I am keeping for myself.
Stop beaming at my cabinet, {winner}. It has enough pressure on it already.
The ribbons are tied and the silver is so bright I can see my future in it.
A draw brings the cups out of the cupboard, which is the next best thing to a win.
The old medals sit beside the new ones, because a good display respects its elders.
I may be stuck in the corner, but the view of your shelves is still rather pleasant, {winner}.
Some evenings it is just the silver and me, and neither of us has to be first.
A soft cloth, a warm bulb and a bit of mild rivalry is all a cabinet needs.
Silver does not tarnish in my house, which is more than I can say for my patience.
No gold changes hands in a draw, so the case keeps its dignity and we keep ours.
Put the medal on the ribbon, then wait for the room to go quiet and admire it properly.
Let us hope the new plate sits straight, {winner}, because I shall be checking it daily.
Gold has its charms, but the quiet click of a cabinet door closing is the real music.
Drawn, we both keep our polish and our pride, which is the most affordable trophy in town.
Handsome cabinet, shining trophies, {winner}. I will sulk in the kitchen, where the spoons are.
The key lives on a chain round my neck, which is the only security system I trust.
The dust is the only thing that wins a draw, so we split the duster down the middle.
Every shelf in this room has a story, and most of them end with me holding a cloth.
I am saving a corner of my shelf for the day I finally get to beat {winner}.
The silver cannot pick a favourite, so we split the polish and I keep the nicer cloth.
I polish my medals in the morning, my cabinet at noon and my ego whenever the room is empty.
{winner} keeps every shelf gleaming, which is an impressive trick for anyone with that much silver.
Engraving is slow work, so I paid for the good letters and let the engraver sulk.
A tie in the trophy room is a fine start to a long conversation about who polishes better.
Your silver looks so bright that I have started wearing sunglasses in my own hallway, {winner}.
Some managers collect stickers, but I collect the little brass plates that say I was here.
A draw is a quiet night in with the silver, and nobody needs a speech.
Ribbons, shelves and a locked door can make a manager feel like royalty for an afternoon.
Let the record show I clapped, polished my glasses and then went straight to the spare key.
Neither trophy goes home today, so we both get the pleasure of dusting them.
The cabinet lock clicks, the light comes on, and suddenly the whole room looks like a museum.
The silver shines so brightly, {winner}, that even my bad mood has started to reflect it.
Keep your head high and your polishing cloth handy, because the trophy room remembers everything.
We both leave the cabinet door ajar, so the silver can hear us being civil.
Trophies forgive being shuffled about the shelves, but they never forgive being ignored.
Honestly, {winner}, I would rather be beaten by you than by the dust, and the dust is winning.
A quiet trophy room is rare, so a draw is the nearest we get to a holiday.
Engraved letters catch the light beautifully, so I stand at an angle to read my own name.
I have decided to frame your trophy room photo, {winner}, so I can scowl at it with dignity.
Nothing has moved, nothing has been won, and the ribbons are still exactly straight.
Place the cup in the middle, step back and let the room applaud you quietly.
Some people judge a manager by the table, but I judge mine by the sparkle on the cups.
Trophies travel well, but the story stays put, so the display gets the best seat.
A draw leaves the trophies unclaimed, so we both get to polish them with clear consciences.
Keep your spare key somewhere safe, {loser}, because the cabinet door is going to need it.
Trophies look better with a little envy around them, {winner}, so thank you for the lovely view.
No names go on the plate after a draw, but it still gets a shine for us both.
I keep a mirror beside the display so I can check my smile, and so can the silver.
The cabinet has better lighting than my living room, {winner}, and I am quietly planning a remodel.
The gold stays put, so the room gets a fresh polish and a grin we share.
A cabinet is for show, but the trophy room is for late nights and a quiet look at it.
